You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
This looks like December 2019. Fed funds at 1.55% fits the post-cuts level, with a 3-month change of -0.58 reflecting cuts from 2.4% in Aug/Sep. The 10-year yield at 1.77% fits too, as does unemployment at 3.6% (it was 3.5% in Dec 2019, 3.6% in Nov 2019 as originally reported). Core CPI at 2.3% matches, and so does headline CPI at 1.77% (Nov 2019 was 2.1% and Dec 2.3%, so those don't fit well).

Checking the alternatives, a headline CPI of 1.77% with core 2.32% could be October 2019: headline was 1.8% and core 2.3%. Fed funds in October 2019 averaged 1.83%, and in November it was 1.55%. So November 2019 fits the policy rate. Unemployment in November was 3.5%, though, and October was 3.6%.

Other data points to November. US equities returned +3.3% in the month, the VIX was 11.75 (it was low in late November/December), and the 10-year yield was 1.77% at the end of November. The 3-month change in payrolls of +175k fits November, and the 3-month change in the 10-year of +0.27 does too (from 1.50 in August).

The headline CPI figure may come from the October release, which would be the latest published in late November. Unemployment at 3.6% would be the October release too, so the data are consistent with the end of November.
